sections.overview: The lingcod is a large northeastern Pacific predator in the greenling family Hexagrammidae, not the cod family Gadidae. It ranges from the Gulf of Alaska to Baja California and may live for more than twenty years.
sections.identification: Its elongated body tapers toward the tail and is mottled grey, brown, green or blue, often with copper spots. A broad, unscaled head and large mouth hold many sharp teeth. Canadian records place maturity near 45 centimetres in males and 61–75 centimetres in females. Some have blue-green flesh that loses colour when cooked; its cause remains unknown. NOAA reports that lingcod can grow to about 1.5 m and 36 kg. These are upper-end values, not typical adult measurements; the cited Canadian maturity lengths are population-specific and do not provide adult sex-specific weights. No reliable body-width measurement was found.
sections.habitat: Adults occupy coastal rocky reefs and other complex bottom habitats, with crevices that provide shelter. Adhesive eggs stay in shallow crevices, and larvae drift near the surface. Juveniles settle on nearshore sand among eelgrass or kelp, then move toward deeper reefs as they grow.
sections.diet: Adults seize prey with a sudden lunge, eating bottom fish—including smaller lingcod—as well as octopuses, squid and crabs. Larvae feed on drifting zooplankton such as krill and tiny crustaceans; juveniles switch to small fish.
sections.behavior: Lingcod remain near familiar reefs; males defend nesting territories in late autumn while females visit spawning grounds seasonally. Sharks, marine mammals and larger lingcod prey on them.
sections.reproduction: Males mature near age two and females near three. In winter and spring, females lay adhesive eggs in rocky crevices; males fertilize and guard them for eight to ten weeks. The eggs hatch into drifting larvae that eat plankton, then settle in coastal nurseries and later feed on fish.
sections.ecology: Rockfish, sculpins, greenlings and sea stars consume unguarded eggs. Young lingcod enter coastal food webs after feeding on surface plankton.
sections.conservation: Commercial and recreational fisheries target lingcod; bottom trawls can disturb habitat and catch other groundfish. NOAA reports both U.S. Pacific stocks were not overfished in 2021 assessments and were not subject to overfishing in 2024. Seasonal closures and limits protect spawning fish.
